name: Digital Forensics
description: Forensic analysis, attack reconstruction, provenance, and incident response.

uss.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection, all from USENIX 2018, set the agenda for modern digital forensics: making attack investigation scale to the kind of long-running campaigns that hide in months of audit logs. "Dependence-Preserving Data Compaction for Scalable Forensic Analysis" (USENIX 2018) attacked the sheer volume problem by shrinking provenance data without losing the causal dependencies investigators need, while "SAQL: A Stream-based Query System for Real-Time Abnormal System Behavior Detection" (USENIX 2018) pushed toward catching abnormal behavior as it happened rather than after the fact. "Enabling Refinable Cross-Host Attack Investigation with Efficient Data Flow Tagging and Tracking" (USENIX 2018) broadened the lens from a single machine to multi-host campaigns, recovering true cross-host dependencies. Alongside system-log forensics, this period also seeded the memory-forensics thread, with "Back to the Whiteboard" (USENIX 2019) calling for a more principled, evaluable foundation for memory analysis techniques.

Around 2020-2021 the field both diversified and embraced learning. "From Control Model to Program: Investigating Robotic Aerial Vehicle Accidents with MAYDAY" (USENIX 2020) extended forensics into cyber-physical accident reconstruction for drones. A 2021 USENIX cohort then matured the provenance-and-log line on several fronts at once: "ATLAS" introduced sequence-based learning to reconstruct attack stories from logs, "SEAL" and "ELISE" tackled storage-efficient causality analysis and logging through compression and representation learning, "CLARION" brought sound provenance tracking to containerized microservices, and "ARCUS" used symbolic execution for root-cause analysis of exploits in production. The same year showed the area's breadth, with malware-capability forecasting from memory images, YARA-based malware intelligence (YARIX), SDN causal analysis, and even physical-world tracing via Moiré patterns (mID).

By 2022-2023 forensics followed computing into new deployment models and confronted the human and adversarial realities of incident response. "ALASTOR: Reconstructing the Provenance of Serverless Intrusions" (USENIX 2022) carried provenance into serverless platforms, while case studies like "The Antrim County 2020 Election Incident" (USENIX 2022) and "Anatomy of a High-Profile Data Breach" (USENIX 2023) grounded the field in real investigations. Learning-driven and cost-aware detection advanced through "DISTDET" and the log-text unsupervised approach "AIRTAG" (both USENIX 2023), and "The Case for Learned Provenance Graph Storage Systems" (USENIX 2023) reframed even storage as a learning problem. Crucially, several 2023 papers turned the lens on the auditing pipeline itself, hardening it against attackers who compromise the OS or starve the audit framework ("Rethinking System Audit Architectures," "Auditing Frameworks Need Resource Isolation"), and "Lessons Lost" (USENIX 2023) examined how cyber insurance and breach attorneys distort incident response in practice.

Most recently, in 2024, the frontier moved toward forensics in adversarial and AI-laden environments. "00SEVen" (USENIX 2024) re-enabled VM forensics inside confidential VMs whose hardware protections otherwise block inspection, and "AI Psychiatry: Forensic Investigation of Deep Learning Networks in Memory Images" (USENIX 2024) opened the investigation of deployed neural networks recovered from memory. A parallel deepfake-forensics thread runs from vocal-tract-based detection (USENIX 2022) to a SoK measuring structural limits of deepfake datasets (USENIX 2024). Taken together, the area has grown from scaling system-log provenance to a multi-front discipline spanning memory, cyber-physical, serverless, confidential-computing, and ML-model forensics, increasingly defending the trustworthiness of the evidence itself.

ndss.narrative:
Digital forensics at NDSS began by attacking a single hard problem: how to reconstruct what an attacker did from noisy system telemetry. The earliest listed work built the causal machinery for this. "Towards a Timely Causality Analysis for Enterprise Security" (NDSS 2018) and "MCI: Modeling-based Causality Inference in Audit Logging for Attack Investigation" (NDSS 2018) chased accurate cause-and-effect chains from audit logs to trace multi-stage APTs, while "Towards Scalable Cluster Auditing through Grammatical Inference over Provenance Graphs" (NDSS 2018) worried about doing this across large distributed systems. At the same time the field was broadening past the enterprise desktop: "Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things" (NDSS 2018) carried provenance into IoT platforms, "JSgraph" (NDSS 2018) reconstructed web attacks from in-browser JavaScript, and "Tipped Off by Your Memory Allocator" (NDSS 2018) sequenced user activity straight out of Android memory images.

The turn from 2019 to 2021 was about making provenance analysis actually deployable. "NoDoze" (NDSS 2019) confronted the practical crisis of alert fatigue by automatically triaging provenance alerts, and provenance graphs became the field's central object: "Unicorn" (NDSS 2020) and "You Are What You Do: Hunting Stealthy Malware via Data Provenance Analysis" (NDSS 2020) used whole-system graphs to catch stealthy, low-and-slow adversaries without signatures. A parallel push improved the raw material and its trustworthiness — "OmegaLog" (NDSS 2020) fused application and system layers to recover semantics, "ALchemist" (NDSS 2021) did similar log fusion without instrumentation, "UIScope" (NDSS 2020) reconstructed attacks on GUI applications, and "Custos" (NDSS 2020) used trusted execution to make audit logs tamper-evident. "WATSON" (NDSS 2021) and "C2SR" (NDSS 2021) then worked on abstracting and reconstructing behavior so human analysts were not drowning in raw events.

By 2022-2023 the community both diversified its targets and began questioning its own foundations. Forensics reached specialized domains — "RVPLAYER" (NDSS 2022) replayed robotic-vehicle accidents with what-if reasoning, "The Truth Shall Set Thee Free" (NDSS 2022) enabled forensics in smart environments, "LogicMEM" (NDSS 2022) and "An OS-agnostic Approach to Memory Forensics" (NDSS 2023) advanced binary-only memory analysis, and "BEAGLE" (NDSS 2023) brought attack forensics to deep-learning backdoors. Crucially, "Sometimes, You Aren't What You Do: Mimicry Attacks against Provenance Graph Host Intrusion Detection Systems" (NDSS 2023) showed these now-standard provenance detectors could be evaded, a sobering robustness check on a decade of graph-based methods.

The most recent work splits along two threads. Real-time, knowledge-driven provenance analysis matured with "NODLINK" (NDSS 2024) doing online fine-grained APT investigation and "KnowHow" (NDSS 2026) automatically applying high-level cyber-threat-intelligence knowledge for interpretable provenance analysis, while "SCRUTINIZER" (NDSS 2025) and "ProvGuard" (NDSS 2025) extended forensics into compromised TrustZone and SDN control planes. The other thread reflects the deepfake era and the rise of LLMs: "VoiceRadar" (NDSS 2025), "Light2Lie" (NDSS 2026), and "Rethinking Fake Speech Detection" (NDSS 2026) push synthetic-media forensics, and "Chimera: Harnessing Multi-Agent LLMs for Automatic Insider Threat Simulation" (NDSS 2026) points to where the field is heading — using multi-agent language models to generate and reason about threats rather than only replaying logs after the fact.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice framed digital forensics as an attack-reconstruction problem to be solved on the fly rather than after the fact. HOLMES (S&P 2019) set the template: correlate suspicious information flows in system audit logs to detect Advanced Persistent Threats in real time, mapping low-level events onto attacker tactics. This kicked off a provenance-graph era, but that approach immediately ran into a scaling wall — the "dependence explosion" where causal graphs balloon into millions of unreadable edges. Tactical Provenance Analysis (S&P 2020) and Combating Dependence Explosion (S&P 2020) attacked this directly, the former distilling graphs into compact tactical summaries for EDR triage and the latter rethinking tag-propagation semantics to keep dependencies tractable; DEPCOMM (S&P 2022) continued the thread by summarizing audit graphs into process-centric communities so a human analyst could actually read them.

The next shift was learning-based. Rather than hand-writing rules over provenance graphs, systems began treating the graph itself as data to learn from. SHADEWATCHER (S&P 2022) reframed threat detection as a recommendation problem over system-entity interactions, and Flash (S&P 2024) and DrSec (S&P 2024) pushed provenance-graph representation learning and distributed embeddings toward comprehensive, efficient endpoint detection. R-CAID (S&P 2024) folded root-cause analysis directly into the detection step so an alert arrives with its explanation attached. Running alongside was a growing self-scrutiny about foundations: SoK: History is a Vast Early Warning System (S&P 2023) took stock of the whole auditing-provenance field, and What We Talk About When We Talk About Logs (S&P 2025) showed how much detection research quietly depends on the quality of its benchmark datasets.

A parallel current worried less about detection and more about whether the evidence can be trusted at all. Because a capable attacker can tamper with the very logs used to catch them, HARDLOG (S&P 2022) introduced a dedicated hardware audit device for tamper-proof logging, and Sealing the Window (S&P 2026) offers efficient tamper protection for provenance logs. Data collection itself became a research target with eAudit (S&P 2024), a fast and deployable audit collector, while broader forensics spread into new substrates: TARDIS (S&P 2020) for CMS attacks, TeSec (S&P 2023) for server-side web-application investigation, Time-Print (S&P 2022) for USB fingerprinting, and studies of data left on discarded IoT devices and police-auctioned phones (both S&P 2023).

The most recent work shows the field splitting toward two frontiers. One is media and content provenance in a deepfake world — VerITAS (S&P 2025) verifies image transformations at scale, Eva (S&P 2025) proves authenticity of lossily encoded videos, and the deepfake-detection analysis (S&P 2024) stress-tests detectors against an evolving threat landscape. The other pushes classic system forensics deeper into the stack and onto new devices: Fine-Grained Kernel Auditing (S&P 2026) augments syscall reference behavior with virtualized selective tracing for far higher-resolution logs, while Recovering and Rehosting Mobile Local LLM Conversations (S&P 2026) opens an entirely new memory-forensics target — reconstructing on-device LLM conversations from memory now that edge devices run models locally. Together, the 2026 work signals a forensics discipline expanding from "reconstruct the intrusion from audit logs" to authenticating digital media and recovering ephemeral AI state.

ccs.narrative:
Digital forensics at CCS has concentrated on system provenance, attack reconstruction, and attribution in both enterprise and blockchain contexts. The 2018 provenance papers established the field's infrastructure: Runtime Analysis of Whole-System Provenance (CCS 2018) captured OS-level causality graphs for root-cause analysis, NodeMerge (CCS 2018) made those graphs tractable at big-data scale, and Large-Scale and Language-Oblivious Code Authorship Identification (CCS 2018) brought authorship attribution to code across programming languages.

Threat hunting operationalized provenance in 2019: POIROT: Aligning Attack Behavior with Kernel Audit Records for Cyber Threat Hunting (CCS 2019) aligned CTI attack graphs with live kernel audit logs to hunt for ongoing intrusions without prior indicators of compromise. Logging to the Danger Zone: Race Condition Attacks and Defenses on System Audit Frameworks (CCS 2020) revealed that audit frameworks themselves are vulnerable to race-condition attacks, undermining forensic integrity.

By 2021-2023, provenance-based forensics reached industrial maturity and faced scaling challenges. BFT Protocol Forensics (CCS 2021) applied forensic reasoning to Byzantine consensus violations in distributed systems. ProvG-Searcher: A Graph Representation Learning Approach for Efficient Provenance Graph Search (CCS 2023) used graph neural networks to efficiently match known APT behavior patterns against large provenance graphs. DE-FAKE (CCS 2023) extended forensic attribution to synthetic media from generative AI.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection, clustered at NDSS 2018, wrestled with a single hard problem: how to reconstruct sophisticated, long-running intrusions from the flood of system audit logs. "Towards a Timely Causality Analysis for Enterprise Security" (NDSS 2018) built the causal dependency graphs that would anchor the whole field, while a parallel line attacked the practical cost of doing so at scale — "Dependence-Preserving Data Compaction for Scalable Forensic Analysis" (USENIX 2018) and "NodeMerge: Template Based Efficient Data Reduction For Big-Data Causality Analysis" (CCS 2018) compressed provenance without destroying the dependencies investigators need, and "Runtime Analysis of Whole-System Provenance" (CCS 2018) pushed capture down into the kernel. Even then the community was branching into related evidence: reconstructing web attacks from in-browser JavaScript ("JSgraph", NDSS 2018) and logging misbehavior in IoT deployments ("Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things", NDSS 2018).

The major shift arrived in 2019-2020, when provenance stopped being just a post-mortem tool and became a real-time detector. "HOLMES" (S&P 2019) correlated suspicious information flows into APT kill chains as they unfolded, "POIROT" (CCS 2019) aligned incoming threat intelligence against audit records for threat hunting, and "NoDoze" (NDSS 2019) tackled the human bottleneck — analyst alert fatigue — by automatically triaging provenance. This period also opened two durable subfields: learning-based detection, seen in "Unicorn" (NDSS 2020) and "You Are What You Do" (NDSS 2020), and the realization that logs must be trustworthy, addressed by tamper-evident auditing in "Custos" (NDSS 2020) and the race-condition defenses of "Logging to the Danger Zone" (CCS 2020). Meanwhile "OmegaLog" (NDSS 2020) and "Combating Dependence Explosion" (S&P 2020) chipped away at the dependency-explosion problem that had haunted causality graphs since 2018.

From 2021 onward the field matured around machine learning and usability. "ATLAS" (USENIX 2021) framed attack reconstruction as sequence learning, "SHADEWATCHER" (S&P 2022) borrowed recommendation-system techniques, and "DEPCOMM" (S&P 2022) and "WATSON" (NDSS 2021) summarized sprawling graphs into human-readable behaviors. By 2023-2024 the community paused to take stock — "SoK: History is a Vast Early Warning System" (S&P 2023) systematized a decade of provenance auditing — and then leaned fully into graph representation learning with "Flash" (S&P 2024).

The most recent work shows the field simultaneously deepening its classic core and spilling into new evidentiary domains. On the provenance side, 2026 brings the LLM turn: "KnowHow" (NDSS 2026) applies high-level CTI knowledge for interpretable analysis, "Chimera" (NDSS 2026) uses multi-agent LLMs to simulate insider threats, and tamper protection and kernel auditing continue to sharpen in "Sealing the Window" (S&P 2026) and "Fine-Grained Kernel Auditing" (S&P 2026). At the same time, "digital forensics" now visibly encompasses media and memory evidence — deepfake image and speech detection in "Light2Lie" and "Rethinking Fake Speech Detection" (both NDSS 2026), ransomware attribution ("High Stakes, Low Certainty", USENIX 2025), and even recovering local LLM conversations through memory forensics ("Recovering and Rehosting Mobile Local LLM Conversations", S&P 2026). The through-line from 2018 remains — turn messy traces into a defensible account of what happened — but the traces and the tools have both grown far richer.
